If your unpaid rent accrued during the COVID-19 emergency period (starting March 1, 2020), your landlord must offer you a repayment plan that limits monthly payments to no more than one-third of your monthly rent for the period of the debt (RCW 59.18.630(2)).

Once the landlord offers you a reasonable repayment plan, you have 14 days to accept it. If you don’t accept the plan within those 14 days, the landlord may start eviction proceedings (unlawful detainer action) (RCW 59.18.630(2)).

If you accepted the repayment plan but have defaulted (missed payments) under that plan, the landlord may seek eviction after giving you a notice of default and a 3-day period to cure or vacate (RCW 59.18.410(3)(c)(iii)(A)).

So:

- If you have not accepted any repayment plan your landlord offered, but it was a reasonable plan and more than 14 days have passed, they can begin eviction.

- If you accepted the plan but missed payments (like being 45 days late), the landlord can serve a notice of default and proceed with eviction after three calendar days if you don’t catch up.

In any eviction proceeding, the court will consider your COVID-related circumstances and the payment plan terms (RCW 59.18.630(2)).

This is legal information, not advice. You may want to consult a lawyer or tenant assistance service to discuss your personal situation.

cases.question: Can my landlord end my lease without a reason after my initial rental period if I signed a one-year lease?
cases.answer:
If you have a one-year lease, the landlord generally cannot end your lease without a reason after the initial period unless specific conditions are met.

According to RCW 59.18.650(1)(b), a landlord may only end a tenancy at the end of the initial lease period without cause if:

1. The original lease was entered into for a term between six and 12 months; and
2. The landlord gave you at least 60 days' advance written notice ending the tenancy before the initial lease expires, served properly under the law.

If these conditions are not met, and your lease ends, the tenancy usually either continues on a month-to-month or another periodic basis, or the landlord must have a legal cause ("cause" is detailed in RCW 59.18.650(2)) to end it.

So, after the initial one-year lease, without proper 60-day written notice or other cause, your landlord cannot simply end your tenancy without reason.

If your lease sets a specific period ("fixed term"), and the landlord meets the notice requirement at the end of that period, then they may end it without cause (as in RCW 59.18.650(1)(c)), but the lease must meet other detailed conditions.

In summary, for a one-year lease, your landlord must provide at least 60 days' written notice before the end of that year to end the lease without cause. Absent that, the lease doesn't just end automatically without reason. This is a general explanation based on the law; for advice about your specific situation, you should consult a lawyer or tenant-rights organization.

cases.question: My landlord wants to start charging a monthly fee instead of a security deposit. Are they allowed to do that?
cases.answer:
Yes, under Washington law, a landlord may offer tenants the option to pay a monthly fee instead of a traditional security deposit, but the tenant's payment of this fee must be strictly optional. The landlord cannot force you to pay the fee; you have the right to choose either a full security deposit or the fee instead (RCW 59.18.670(1)(a)).

Moreover, if the landlord offers this fee option, they must provide it fairly and equally to all approved applicants without discrimination based on income, credit score, race, gender, or other protected characteristics (RCW 59.18.670(1)(c)). The landlord must also disclose in writing specific information about the fee, including that it is not refundable and does not count as rent, along with details about any insurance coverage the landlord obtains to cover losses related to unpaid rent or damages beyond ordinary wear and tear (RCW 59.18.670(1)(f)).

So, in summary, your landlord can offer a monthly fee instead of a security deposit, but you must be allowed to choose to pay a traditional deposit if you prefer, and the landlord must provide proper disclosures and treat all tenants fairly according to RCW 59.18.670.

cases.question: My landlord tried to raise my rent by 12% during my first year, is that allowed?
cases.answer:
No, your landlord cannot raise your rent by 12% during your first year of tenancy. Under RCW 59.18.700(1)(a)(i), landlords may not increase the rent during the first 12 months after the tenancy begins. This means no rent increase is allowed in that time frame regardless of the percentage.

If the rent increase is applied and it is not authorized by an exemption under RCW 59.18.710, you have remedies. You can provide your landlord written notice demanding the increase be reduced to comply with the law, and you may terminate the rental agreement by giving at least 20 days' written notice before the increase takes effect, without penalty, paying rent for the full month you move out (RCW 59.18.700(3)).

If you want to proceed, you should be sure to put your concerns in writing to the landlord. This information is legal information, not legal advice, and you may want to consult a lawyer or tenant rights group for personal guidance.

cases.question: Can my landlord increase my rent more than 7% plus the consumer price index in a year?
cases.answer:
Generally, your landlord **cannot increase your rent more than 7% plus the consumer price index (CPI), or 10%, whichever is less, in any 12-month period** after the first year of your tenancy. Also, rent cannot be increased at all during the first 12 months of your tenancy (RCW 59.18.700(1)(a)(i) and (ii)).

However, there are some **exemptions** (RCW 59.18.710). For example, if your rental unit is:

- A newer building issued a certificate of occupancy 12 years ago or less,
- Owned by a public housing authority or nonprofit organization regulated by affordable housing laws,
- An owner-occupied single-family home with no more than two rental units,
- Or certain other housing types described in RCW 59.18.710,

then your landlord may legally raise rent above this limit. If so, the landlord must clearly indicate this exemption and provide supporting facts in the written rent increase notice (RCW 59.18.720).

If your landlord raises your rent above the allowed limit **without a proper exemption** and notice, you can demand in writing that the landlord reduce the increase to the legal limit. You may also choose to terminate your rental agreement by giving notice at least 20 days before ending the tenancy, paying rent through your last month (RCW 59.18.700(3)).

So, unless your landlord qualifies for an exemption and properly notifies you, they cannot increase your rent more than 7% plus CPI or 10% annually after your first year of tenancy.

cases.question: Can my landlord raise the rent more than usual if I just moved in within the last year?
cases.answer:
No, your landlord generally cannot raise your rent more than the usual limit during the first 12 months after your tenancy begins. Specifically, under RCW 59.18.700(1)(a)(i), a landlord may not increase rent during the first 12 months after the tenancy starts, except for certain exemptions described in RCW 59.18.710.

So if you just moved in within the past year, your landlord can't raise your rent until that 12-month period completes, unless your situation falls within one of the exemptions like:

- Your unit's first certificate of occupancy was issued 12 or fewer years ago (a newer building),
- Or your landlord meets other specific exempt criteria under RCW 59.18.710.

If your landlord tries to raise the rent more than allowed before the 12 months are up and without a proper exemption, such an increase would not be lawful.

cases.question: If I rent a single-family home owned by the owner, can my landlord increase the rent more than what the law normally allows?
cases.answer:
Yes. According to RCW 59.18.710(1)(f), rent increase limits do not apply to tenancies in single-family owner-occupied residences. This means the landlord of a single-family home who lives there (owner-occupied) can increase rent more than the usual limits in RCW 59.18.700.

However, the exemption only applies if the owner is a natural person and not a corporation, real estate investment trust, or certain LLCs as described in RCW 59.18.710(2).

So, if you rent a single-family home where the owner lives there as their main residence and the owner is not a corporation or similar entity, your landlord is exempt from the normal rent increase limits and can raise your rent more than normally allowed under state law. The landlord would still need to give you proper written notice of any increase. 

This is not legal advice, just information based on the statute.

cases.question: Can my landlord raise my rent more than 7% plus inflation in a year?
cases.answer:
Under Washington state law, your landlord generally cannot raise your rent more than 7% plus the consumer price index (inflation) in any 12-month period, or 10%, whichever is less, during your tenancy (RCW 59.18.700(1)(a)(ii)). Also, rent increases are not allowed during the first 12 months of your tenancy unless there's an exemption (RCW 59.18.700(1)(a)(i)).

However, there are some exemptions where landlords can raise rent more than this limit. Examples include:

- The dwelling unit is relatively new (certificate of occupancy issued 12 or fewer years ago).
- The property is owned by certain public or nonprofit housing authorities or has specific affordable housing regulations.
- The tenant shares facilities with an owner who lives on the property.
- The rental unit is part of a single-family owner-occupied home or certain small multi-unit residences (duplex, triplex, or fourplex) where the owner lives on site (RCW 59.18.710).

If your landlord claims an exemption to raise rent beyond the usual limit, they must provide written notice to you, including facts to support the exemption (RCW 59.18.720(2), (3)).

So, unless your landlord qualifies for and properly notifies you of an exemption, they cannot legally raise your rent more than 7% plus inflation or 10%, whichever is less, within a 12-month period.

cases.question: My landlord says they can increase my rent by more than 10% because I live in a duplex; is that OK?
cases.answer:
Whether your landlord can raise your rent by more than 10% because you live in a duplex depends on specific conditions.

Under RCW 59.18.710(1)(g), landlords may raise rent above the usual limit for tenancies in a duplex, triplex, or fourplex **only if** the owner occupied one of the units as their principal residence at the beginning of the tenancy and continues to occupy that unit. Additionally, per RCW 59.18.710(2), this exemption only applies if the owner is **not** a corporation, real estate investment trust, or LLC with a corporate member.

So, if your duplex landlord:

- Lives in one of the units as their main home since your tenancy began and still does, and
- Is an individual owner, not a corporate entity,

then the landlord may lawfully increase rent by more than the usual limits.

If these conditions are not met, the normal rent increase limits still apply (up to 7% plus inflation or 10%, whichever is less, once every 12 months under RCW 59.18.700), and any larger increase might be unlawful.

You can ask your landlord for proof that they qualify for this exemption, which they must provide if they claim it in a rent increase notice form under RCW 59.18.720.

If your landlord raises rent beyond allowed limits without a valid exemption, you have the right to demand a reduction or choose to end your lease early without penalty (RCW 59.18.700(3)).

This is legal information, not advice. If you want to pursue this, consider consulting a tenant rights professional or legal aid.

cases.question: My window is a necessary exit, can I put a portable air conditioner in that window without any problems?
cases.answer:
If your window is a necessary exit (egress), the landlord can prohibit or restrict you from installing a window-mounted portable cooling device there if the device would interfere with using the window as a way to exit the dwelling (RCW 59.18.740(4)(a)(i)). 

This means if the air conditioner blocks or makes it harder to use that window to exit in an emergency, the landlord can say no to installing it in that window.

So, to answer your question: You generally cannot install a window-mounted portable air conditioner in a window that is a necessary exit if the device would interfere with the window’s use as an exit. You might be able to install it elsewhere, or use a type of portable cooling device that does not block the egress. 

Remember also that you must provide your landlord with at least two days' notice before installation (RCW 59.18.740(6)).

This is legal information, not advice. If you want to know what you specifically should do, consider consulting a lawyer or tenant support organizations.

cases.question: Can my landlord stop me from installing a portable AC unit in my apartment?
cases.answer:
Under Washington's tenant law (RCW 59.18.740), your landlord generally cannot stop you from installing a portable cooling device like a portable AC unit of your choice.

However, there are some exceptions where your landlord can restrict or prohibit installation:

- If your dwelling already has a permanently installed and fully operational heat pump.
- If the installation would violate building codes, laws, or the device’s safety guidelines.
- If installation would cause unreasonable damage or make the apartment uninhabitable.
- If your electrical system cannot safely support the device.

If the AC is window-mounted, your landlord can also restrict it if:

- It blocks a necessary escape window.
- It interferes with locking windows accessible from outside.
- It causes damage to the window or building.
- It cannot be secured safely.
- The landlord's insurance prohibits window-mounted ACs (and the landlord must show you proof of this).

So, unless one of those specific exceptions applies, your landlord cannot stop you from putting in a portable AC unit. Also, your landlord cannot charge a fee just for you installing or using the unit, though they can charge for any damages caused (RCW 59.18.740(1), (3), (4), (2)).

Remember, you must give the landlord at least two days' notice before installing a window-mounted AC (RCW 59.18.740(6)).

This is general legal information based on the statute; for advice about your personal situation, you might want to contact a tenant rights organization or attorney.

cases.question: What kind of privacy information does my landlord have to give me about the smart access system?
cases.answer:
Your landlord must provide you a clear, written privacy policy about the smart access system either when you sign your lease or within five days after the system is installed. This policy must be in plain language and include at least the following information:

1. What data the system collects, including any data about your guests (RCW 59.18.755(2)(a)).

2. How your landlord will protect that data with security measures (RCW 59.18.755(2)(b)).

3. How long the data will be kept before being destroyed or anonymized (RCW 59.18.755(2)(c)).

4. What the landlord will do if there is an unauthorized access or breach of your data, including how and when you will be notified (RCW 59.18.755(2)(d)).

5. Guidelines on permanently destroying or anonymizing data or removing it from the system (RCW 59.18.755(2)(e)).

6. The process for adding a tenant temporarily to the system if they give written consent (RCW 59.18.755(2)(f)).

If the landlord uses a smart access system developer's privacy policy and does not keep or sell any data themselves, they may simply give you that developer's written policy or a link to it instead (RCW 59.18.755(3)).

This law starts applying from January 1, 2027 (RCW 59.18.755).

So basically, you should receive clear explained details about what info is gathered, how it’s safeguarded, how long it’s held, what happens if a data breach occurs, and how temporary user additions work. This ensures transparency and protects your privacy rights.

cases.question: My landlord just installed a smart access system and gave me a privacy policy. Do I need to also get details about how my data is protected and how long it will be kept?
cases.answer:
Yes, under Washington's Residential Landlord-Tenant Act (RCW 59.18.755), when your landlord installs a smart access system, they must provide you with a clear written privacy policy. This policy must include details such as:

- What data the system collects (including any information about your guests),
- How your data will be protected,
- How long your data will be retained,
- What will happen if there is a security breach (including how tenants will be notified), and
- How data will be permanently destroyed or anonymized.

Your landlord must give you this written policy either when you initially sign your lease or within five days of installing the smart access system (RCW 59.18.755(1) and (2)). So yes, you should receive information not only about the data collected but also about data protection and retention.

If you did not get this information, you may want to ask your landlord specifically for these details, since the law requires it.

cases.question: If I signed a one-year lease that ends next month, how much notice does my landlord have to give me before increasing the rent?
cases.answer:
If your one-year lease ends next month, your landlord must give you written notice of any rent increase at least **60 days** before the increase's effective date, according to RCW 59.18.140(3)(c). This applies when a lease or rental agreement was entered into or renewed before May 7, 2025, and has between 60 and 90 days left before the lease term ends as of that date.

So, since your lease has just about a month left (which is fewer than 60 days), your landlord should still provide 60 days' written notice before increasing rent for any new lease term or renewal starting after your current lease ends.

In summary, your landlord must give you at least 60 days' written notice before charging a higher rent once your current lease expires.

cases.question: Can my landlord ask me for sexual favors in exchange for a better rental term?
cases.answer:

While the exact statute you mention isn't included in the provided extracts, under RCW 59.18.650(2)(p), a landlord may terminate a tenancy with proper notice if a tenant has made unwanted sexual advances or harassment toward others, implying that sexual harassment in the landlord-tenant relationship is recognized as improper conduct.

Moreover, any lease provisions trying to waive your rights or require something illegal (like sexual favors) would be unenforceable under RCW 59.18.230, which forbids clauses that waive tenant rights or include illegal terms.

If you face such conduct, it is important to seek legal advice or support organizations as well, since this situation involves serious misconduct beyond typical landlord-tenant disputes.
